sentences.text: Adamantinasuchus was a tiny crocodylomorph, measuring only about 0.50 centimeters in length, with a skull roughly 60 millimeters long and 30 millimeters high.
Its skull featured very large elliptical orbits nearly as long as the snout, a trait suggesting the animal might have been nocturnal.
The teeth were noticeably heterodont, mixing incisiform, caniniform, and molariform types where sharp front teeth cut food and posterior molar-like teeth crushed it.
The animal possessed eye sockets measuring approximately 60 millimeters in length and 30 in height, which were nearly as long as the rostrum.
Its dentition included a mixture of tooth shapes, with sharp front teeth for cutting and posterior molar-like teeth for crushing.
The genus is known from a single holotype fossil collected by William Nava, giving the species its specific name navae.
Remains were discovered in the Adamantina Formation near Marília, São Paulo, Brazil, during dam construction 25 km southwest of Marilia.
Excavations yielded approximately 7 specimens, mostly cranial material, some postcranial parts, and dozens of isolated bone elements.
Researchers suggest Adamantinasuchus might have had an omnivorous diet including plants, similar to Chimaerasuchus, due to its heterodont teeth and well-developed molariform teeth.

However, due to insufficient preservation of key jaw bones, it is debated whether Adamantinasuchus could chew plants; the lack of wear on its teeth suggests it was likely only capable of dorsoventral biting motions and ate softer food than plants.
It was likely a carnivore or omnivore that fed on small vertebrates or animal carcasses.
Adamantinasuchus belongs to the suborder Notosuchia and is classified within the unranked family Ziphosuchia.
While occasionally classified in the family Sphagesauridae, some phylogenetic analyses suggest it is closely related to the genera Yacarerani or Pakasuchus rather than Sphagesaurus.
Adamantinasuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Brazil, with fossils dating to the Turonian or Santonian ages or recorded as Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago).
